claim: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is the most common inherited ataxia.
source: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), the most common inherited ataxia, is caused by recessive mutations that reduce the levels of frataxin (FXN), a mitochondrial iron binding protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: FRDA is caused by recessive mutations that reduce the levels of frataxin (FXN).
source: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), the most common inherited ataxia, is caused by recessive mutations that reduce the levels of frataxin (FXN), a mitochondrial iron binding protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Frataxin (FXN) is a mitochondrial iron binding protein.
source: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), the most common inherited ataxia, is caused by recessive mutations that reduce the levels of frataxin (FXN), a mitochondrial iron binding protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge about FXN function.

claim: The authors developed an inducible mouse model of Fxn deficiency.
source: We developed an inducible mouse model of Fxn deficiency that enabled us to control the onset and progression of disease phenotypes by the modulation of Fxn levels.
evidence: This is the primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: The inducible mouse model enables control of the onset and progression of disease phenotypes by modulation of Fxn levels.
source: We developed an inducible mouse model of Fxn deficiency that enabled us to control the onset and progression of disease phenotypes by the modulation of Fxn levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental design showing doxycycline-dependent Fxn knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Systemic knockdown of Fxn in adult mice led to multiple phenotypes paralleling those observed in human patients across multiple organ systems.
source: Systemic knockdown of Fxn in adult mice led to multiple phenotypes paralleling those observed in human patients across multiple organ systems.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral, physiological, and pathological data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: Upon restoration of near wild-type FXN levels, significant recovery of function, associated pathology and transcriptomic dysregulation was observed even after substantial motor dysfunction and pathology.
source: Remarkably, upon restoration of near wild-type FXN levels, we observed significant recovery of function, associated pathology and transcriptomic dysregulation even after substantial motor dysfunction and pathology were observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figures 2-8 with behavioral, pathological, and transcriptomic data.

claim: A guanine-adenine-adenine (GAA) trinucleotide repeat expansion within the first intron of the frataxin (Fxn) gene in chromosome 9 is the major cause of Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA).
source: A guanine-adenine-adenine (GAA) trinucleotide repeat expansion within the first intron of the frataxin (Fxn) gene in the chromosome 9 is the major cause of Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), the most commonly inherited ataxia (Chamberlain et al., 1988; Campuzano et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chamberlain et al., 1988 and Campuzano et al., 1996.

claim: The GAA repeat expansion causes a marked deficiency of Fxn mRNA and protein levels due to reduced Fxn gene transcription.
source: Due to recessive inheritance of this GAA repeat expansion, patients have a marked deficiency of Fxn mRNA and protein levels caused by reduced Fxn gene transcription (Campuzano et al., 1996; Campuzano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campuzano et al., 1996 and 1997.

claim: The GAA expansion size correlates with residual Fxn levels, earlier onset, and increased severity of disease.
source: Indeed, the GAA expansion size has been shown to correlate with residual Fxn levels, earlier onset, and increased severity of disease (Filla et al., 1996; Montermini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filla et al., 1996 and Montermini et al., 1997.

claim: The prevalence of heterozygous carriers of the GAA expansion is between 1:60 and 1:110 in European populations.
source: The prevalence of heterozygous carriers of the GAA expansion is between 1:60 and 1:110 in European populations, and the heterozygous carriers of a Fxn mutation are not clinically affected (Andermann et al., 1976; Harding, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andermann et al., 1976 and Harding, 1981.

claim: Heterozygous carriers of a Fxn mutation are not clinically affected.
source: The prevalence of heterozygous carriers of the GAA expansion is between 1:60 and 1:110 in European populations, and the heterozygous carriers of a Fxn mutation are not clinically affected (Andermann et al., 1976; Harding, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andermann et al., 1976 and Harding, 1981.

claim: FRDA is an early-onset neurodegenerative disease that progressively impairs motor function.
source: FRDA is an early-onset neurodegenerative disease that progressively impairs motor function, leading to ataxic gait, cardiac abnormalities, and other medical co-morbidities, ultimately resulting in early mortality (median age of death, 35 years) (Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013; Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013 and Koeppen, 2011.

claim: FRDA leads to ataxic gait, cardiac abnormalities, and other medical co-morbidities.
source: FRDA is an early-onset neurodegenerative disease that progressively impairs motor function, leading to ataxic gait, cardiac abnormalities, and other medical co-morbidities, ultimately resulting in early mortality (median age of death, 35 years) (Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013; Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013 and Koeppen, 2011.

claim: FRDA results in early mortality with a median age of death of 35 years.
source: FRDA is an early-onset neurodegenerative disease that progressively impairs motor function, leading to ataxic gait, cardiac abnormalities, and other medical co-morbidities, ultimately resulting in early mortality (median age of death, 35 years) (Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013; Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koeppen and Mazurkiewicz, 2013 and Koeppen, 2011.

claim: Patients with late onset FRDA tend to have slower progression with less severe phenotype and are associated with smaller GAA expansions.
source: However, identification of the causal gene led to identification of a significant number of patients with late onset, tend to have slower progression with less severe phenotype and are associated with smaller GAA expansions (Bhidayasiri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhidayasiri et al., 2005.

claim: Shorter GAA expansion enables residual Fxn expression.
source: This shorter expansion enables residual Fxn expression (Li et al., 2015), thus modifying the classical FRDA phenotype, consistent with other data indicating that Fxn deficiency is directly related to the FRDA phenotype (Seibler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2015 and Seibler et al., 2005.

claim: Fxn deficiency is directly related to the FRDA phenotype.
source: This shorter expansion enables residual Fxn expression (Li et al., 2015), thus modifying the classical FRDA phenotype, consistent with other data indicating that Fxn deficiency is directly related to the FRDA phenotype (Seibler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seibler et al., 2005.

claim: Metabolic dysfunction and insulin intolerance are observed in the majority of FRDA patients.
source: Extra-neurologic symptoms including metabolic dysfunction and insulin intolerance are observed in the majority and frank type I diabetes is observed in approximately 15% of patients, the severity of which is related to increasing repeat length (Martinez et al., 2017; Galea et al., 2016; Coppola et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2017, Galea et al., 2016, and Coppola et al., 2009.

claim: Frank type I diabetes is observed in approximately 15% of FRDA patients.
source: Extra-neurologic symptoms including metabolic dysfunction and insulin intolerance are observed in the majority and frank type I diabetes is observed in approximately 15% of patients, the severity of which is related to increasing repeat length (Martinez et al., 2017; Galea et al., 2016; Coppola et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2017, Galea et al., 2016, and Coppola et al., 2009.

claim: The severity of diabetes in FRDA is related to increasing GAA repeat length.
source: Extra-neurologic symptoms including metabolic dysfunction and insulin intolerance are observed in the majority and frank type I diabetes is observed in approximately 15% of patients, the severity of which is related to increasing repeat length (Martinez et al., 2017; Galea et al., 2016; Coppola et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2017, Galea et al., 2016, and Coppola et al., 2009.

claim: FXN is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein involved in the biogenesis of iron-sulphur clusters.
source: FXN is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein involved in the biogenesis of iron-sulphur clusters, which are important for the function of the mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Abrahão et al., 2015; Tanaka et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abrahão et al., 2015 and Tanaka et al., 1996.

claim: Iron-sulphur clusters are important for the function of the mitochondrial respiratory chain activity.
source: FXN is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein involved in the biogenesis of iron-sulphur clusters, which are important for the function of the mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Abrahão et al., 2015; Tanaka et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abrahão et al., 2015 and Tanaka et al., 1996.

claim: Homozygous frataxin knockout mice display embryonic lethality.
source: Studies in mouse have shown that Fxn plays an important role during embryonic development, as homozygous frataxin knockout mice display embryonic lethality (Cossée et al., 2000), consistent with FXN's evolutionary conservation from yeast to human (Campuzano et al., 1996; Campuzano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cossée et al., 2000.

claim: FXN is evolutionarily conserved from yeast to human.
source: Studies in mouse have shown that Fxn plays an important role during embryonic development, as homozygous frataxin knockout mice display embryonic lethality (Cossée et al., 2000), consistent with FXN's evolutionary conservation from yeast to human (Campuzano et al., 1996; Campuzano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campuzano et al., 1996 and 1997.

claim: Multiple mouse models of frataxin deficiency have been generated including knock-in knockout, repeat expansion knock-in, transgenic YG8R and YG22R, and conditional knockout models.
source: Over the past several years, multiple mouse models of frataxin deficiency, including a knock-in knockout model (Miranda et al., 2002), repeat expansion knock-in model (Miranda et al., 2002), transgenic mice containing the entire Fxn gene within a human yeast artificial chromosome, YG8R and YG22R (Al-Mahdawi et al., 2004; Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006), as well as a conditional Fxn knockout mouse, including the cardiac-specific (Puccio et al., 2001) and a neuron specific model (Puccio et al., 2001) have been generated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miranda et al., 2002, Al-Mahdawi et al., 2004, 2006, and Puccio et al., 2001.

claim: Existing transgenic and heterozygous knockout FRDA animal models are either mildly symptomatic or restricted in their ability to recapitulate the spatial and temporal aspects of systemic FRDA pathology.
source: These existing transgenic and heterozygous knockout FRDA animal models are either mildly symptomatic or restricted in their ability to recapitulate the spatial and temporal aspects of systemic FRDA pathology when they are engineered as tissue-specific conditional knockouts (Miranda et al., 2002; Al-Mahdawi et al., 2004; Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006; Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Perdomini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous mouse models.

claim: The authors employed recombinase-mediated cassette exchange for genomic integration of a single copy shRNA transgene.
source: We employed recombinase-mediated cassette exchange for genomic integration of a single copy shRNA transgene (doxycycline-inducible) that can mediate frataxin silencing temporally under the control of the H1 promoter via its insertion in a defined genomic locus that is widely expressed (rosa26 ) (Seibler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is described in the methods and supported by citation to Seibler et al., 2007.

claim: The shRNA transgene is doxycycline-inducible and inserted into the rosa26 locus.
source: We employed recombinase-mediated cassette exchange for genomic integration of a single copy shRNA transgene (doxycycline-inducible) that can mediate frataxin silencing temporally under the control of the H1 promoter via its insertion in a defined genomic locus that is widely expressed (rosa26 ) (Seibler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Temporal Fxn knockdown was achieved depending on the dose of doxycycline.
source: Depending on the dose of the inductor doxycycline (dox), temporal Fxn knockdown was achieved to control the onset and progression of the disease (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments described in the methods.

claim: Six different shRNA sequences were screened in vitro to obtain a highly efficient shRNA targeting the mature coding sequence of frataxin.
source: Six different shRNA sequences were screened in vitro to obtain a highly efficient shRNA targeting the mature coding sequence of frataxin (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The shRNA sequence GGATGGCGTGCTCACCATTAA was selected for generating the transgenic animal.
source: We selected the most efficient shRNA (GGATGGCGTGCTCACCATTAA) for validation and generating the transgenic animal.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Fxn is the earliest gene product reduced at the transcriptomic level after shRNA induction.
source: We observe that Fxn is the earliest gene product reduced at the transcriptomic level, and does not alter the expression levels of other potential targets (9 genes with 13–16 nucleotide matches; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with the shRNA's specificity for Fxn.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with gene expression data.

claim: The combination of 2 mg/ml doxycycline in drinking water coupled with 5 or 10 mg/kg intraperitoneal injection twice per week led to efficient Fxn knockdown within two weeks.
source: We found that the combination of 2 mg/ml in drinking water coupled with 5 or 10 mg/kg intraperitoneal injection of dox twice per week led to efficient Fxn knockdown within two weeks post treatment initiation, while avoiding a high early mortality rate (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1f,g.

claim: Greater than 90% Fxn knockdown was achieved across multiple CNS and non-CNS tissues after 20 weeks of doxycycline treatment.
source: Following 20 weeks with (Tg +) or without (Tg -) doxycycline administration (Figure 1c; Materials and methods), we observed highly efficient silencing of Fxn, reaching greater than 90% knockdown across multiple CNS and non-CNS tissues (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d,e with Western blot quantification.

claim: Efficient Fxn silencing was observed as early as three weeks after doxycycline treatment.
source: Using this regimen, time series western blot analyses of 80 independent animals (wildtype with dox (Wt +) N = 24; transgenic with dox (Tg +) N = 24; transgenic without dox (Tg -) N = 24; transgenic with dox removal (Rescue Tg ±) N = 8, at weeks 0, 3, 8, 12, 16, and 20) confirmed efficient silencing as early as three weeks, and efficient rescue, as evidenced by normal frataxin levels, post eight weeks dox removal (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f,g with time series Western blot data.

claim: Normal frataxin levels were restored eight weeks after doxycycline removal.
source: Using this regimen, time series western blot analyses of 80 independent animals (wildtype with dox (Wt +) N = 24; transgenic with dox (Tg +) N = 24; transgenic without dox (Tg -) N = 24; transgenic with dox removal (Rescue Tg ±) N = 8, at weeks 0, 3, 8, 12, 16, and 20) confirmed efficient silencing as early as three weeks, and efficient rescue, as evidenced by normal frataxin levels, post eight weeks dox removal (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f,g with Western blot data.

claim: FRDAkd mice exhibited significant weight loss at 25 weeks with doxycycline treatment.
source: We observed significant weight loss and reduced survival ratio (<90%) at 25 weeks with dox treatment in Fxn knockdown animals (Tg +) compared to other control groups (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a with body weight measurements over time.

claim: FRDAkd mice showed reduced survival ratio (<90%) at 25 weeks with doxycycline treatment.
source: We observed significant weight loss and reduced survival ratio (<90%) at 25 weeks with dox treatment in Fxn knockdown animals (Tg +) compared to other control groups (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with survival curve data.

claim: Tg + mice exhibited shorter distance travelled at both 12 and 24 weeks compared to control animals.
source: Tg + mice exhibited a shorter distance travelled at both 12 and 24 weeks in comparison to control animals, consistent with decreased locomotor activity (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c with open field test data.

claim: Fxn knockdown mice displayed reduced hind and front limb stride length at 12 and 24 weeks, suggesting ataxic gait.
source: The Fxn knockdown mice (Tg +) displayed reduced hind and front limb stride length when compared with Tg-, as well as the Wt control + at 12 and 24 weeks, suggesting ataxic gait (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2d,e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d,e with gait analysis data.

claim: Tg + animals displayed defects in forelimb muscular strength at 12 and 24 weeks.
source: Grip strength testing also showed that Tg + animals displayed defects in their forelimb muscular strength at 12 and 24 weeks when compared with other groups (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2f with grip strength test data.

claim: Chronically treated Tg + mice fell significantly faster on the Rotarod test from 12 weeks onward, indicative of motor impairments.
source: Whereas no significant difference in time spent on the rod before falling off was seen between Wt + or Wt - or Tg - and Tg ± mice after 12 weeks post dox removal (rescue), chronically treated mice (Tg +mice) from 12 weeks onward fell significantly faster, indicative of motor impairments (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 2g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2g with Rotarod test data.

claim: The ECG of Tg + mice displayed a significant increase in QT interval duration at both 12 and 24 weeks post dox treatment.
source: The ECG of Tg + mice displayed a significant increase in QT interval duration when compared to the other control/comparison groups at both 12 and 24 weeks post dox treatment, suggesting abnormal heart rate and rhythm (arrhythmia) (Surawicz and Knoebel, 1984) (Materials and methods; p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 3a–b,e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a,b,e with ECG data.

claim: Rescue animals (Tg ±) showed a normal ECG 12 weeks after dox removal.
source: However, rescue animals (Tg ±) 12 weeks after dox removal showed a normal ECG, demonstrating that by restoring FXN levels, the prolonged QT interval can recover (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 3b,e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b,e with ECG data from rescue animals.

claim: Tg + animals at week 24 displayed absence of P-waves, suggesting an atrial conduction abnormality.
source: We also observed that the Tg +animals at week 24 displayed absence of P-waves, suggesting an atrial conduction abnormality (German et al., 2016) (Figure 3c), not observed in the rescued animals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c with ECG traces and supported by citation to German et al., 2016.

claim: By 24 weeks, dox treated transgenic animals (Tg +) exhibited ventricular and posterior wall thickening.
source: However, by 24 weeks, dox treated transgenic animals (Tg +) exhibited ventricular and posterior wall thickening, suggesting hypertrophic cardiomyopathy when compared to other control groups (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 3d,f,g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d,f,g with echocardiogram data.

claim: Substantially increased myocardial iron was observed in Tg + mice at 20 weeks.
source: Indeed, we observed substantially increased myocardial iron in Tg + mice, as evidenced by increased ferric iron staining (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the increased expression of iron metabolic proteins, ferritin and ferroportin, at 20 weeks (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a,b with iron staining and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Excessive collagen deposition was revealed in Tg + mice hearts at 20 weeks, suggesting cardiac fibrosis.
source: Histological analysis by Masson's trichrome staining revealed excessive collagen deposition in Tg + mice hearts at 20 weeks when compared to other control groups, suggesting cardiac fibrosis (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c with Masson's trichrome staining.

claim: Tg + mice demonstrate severe disorganization with disordered and irregular sarcomeres with enlarged mitochondria at 20 weeks.
source: In contrast, Tg + mice demonstrate severe disorganization, displaying disordered and irregular sarcomeres with enlarged mitochondria at 20 weeks (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d with electron microscopy images.

claim: Mitochondria with disorganized cristae and vacuoles were observed in Tg + mouse heart at 20 weeks.
source: In a minority of cases, but never in controls, we observed mitochondria with disorganized cristae and vacuoles in Tg + mouse heart at 20 weeks, suggesting mitochondrial degeneration (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e with electron microscopy images.

claim: Decreased aconitase activity was observed in the Tg + mouse heart at 20 weeks.
source: Next, by examining aconitase, an Fe-S containing enzyme whose activity is reduced in FRDA patients (Bradley et al., 2000; Rötig et al., 1997), activities in Tg + and other control groups, we observed decreased aconitase activity in the Tg + mouse heart at 20 weeks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4f with aconitase activity assay data and supported by citations to Bradley et al., 2000 and Rötig et al., 1997.

claim: A significant increase in condensed mitochondria was detected in DRG neurons of Tg + mice at 20 weeks.
source: As anticipated, no mitochondrial abnormalities were detected in DRG neurons in the control groups, but a significant increase in condensed mitochondria were detected in DRG neurons of Tg + mice at 20 weeks (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 5), but not in Tg - or Wt + mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with electron microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Empty vesicles associated with condensed mitochondria were observed in DRG neurons of Tg + animals.
source: In most case, we observed empty vesicles associated with condensed mitochondria in DRG neurons of Tg + animals, but not in other control groups, suggesting neuronal degeneration, similar to what is observed in FRDA patients (Koeppen, 2011) (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Materials and methods; Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b,c with electron microscopy images and supported by citation to Koeppen, 2011.

claim: Significant reduction in axonal size and myelin sheath thickness was observed in the spinal cord samples of Tg + mice at 20 weeks.
source: By analyzing more than 2000 axons per group in the lumbar spinal cord cross-section of high-resolution electron micrographs, we observed significant reduction in axonal size and myelin sheath thickness in the spinal cord samples of Tg + mice when compared to other control groups at 20 weeks (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA; Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a-c with electron microscopy images and quantification.

claim: The number of Purkinje cells and the cerebellar granular and molecular layers were not altered due to Fxn knockdown at 20 weeks.
source: In the cerebellum, the number of Purkinje cells and the cerebellar granular and molecular layers were not altered due to Fxn knockdown at 20 weeks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with histological analysis.

claim: Disruption of photoreceptors was observed in Tg + mice at 20 weeks.
source: By electron microscopic examination of the photoreceptors in the retina, which are specialized neurons capable of phototransduction, we observed disruption in Tg + mice at 20 weeks (Materials and methods; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6d with electron microscopy images.

claim: A significant increase in degenerating RPE cells with vacuoles was found in Tg + mice.
source: Similarly, we also found a significant increase in degenerating RPE cells with vacuoles in Tg + mice, which is involved in light absorption and maintenance of visual function (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6e with electron microscopy images.

claim: No changes in the phosphorylation of S241 in the PDK1 activation loop were observed after chronic adult Fxn knockdown.
source: We measured pPDK levels in brain, muscle, heart, and liver samples after chronic adult Fxn knockdown, but did not observe changes in the phosphorylation of S241 in the PDK1 activation loop, which is required for its activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with Western blot data.

claim: Sgca was significantly over-expressed after Fxn knockdown in the cerebellum.
source: In two independent experiments, each utilizing four biological replicates, we found that Sgca (one of five genes tested) was significantly over-expressed after Fxn knockdown in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with RT-PCR data.

claim: Nr4a1 was significantly over-expressed in the heart after Fxn knockdown.
source: In the heart, we found Nr4a1 was significantly over-expressed, while two of the other Mef2c targets, Hrc and Tcap, were significantly down-regulated after Fxn knockdown.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with RT-PCR data.

claim: Hrc and Tcap were significantly down-regulated in the heart after Fxn knockdown.
source: In the heart, we found Nr4a1 was significantly over-expressed, while two of the other Mef2c targets, Hrc and Tcap, were significantly down-regulated after Fxn knockdown.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 with RT-PCR data.

claim: No changes in 3-nitrotyrosine (3NT) and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) levels were observed on brain, liver, and muscle samples from Wt + and Tg + mice at 12 and 20 weeks.
source: To address this in our adult onset model, we first measured the levels of two markers of oxidative stress, 3-nitrotyrosine (3NT) and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), on brain, liver, and muscle samples from the Wt + and Tg + mice at 12 and 20 weeks, and did not observe any changes in these markers.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 with Western blot data.

claim: No evidence for increases in levels of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (DNP-hydrazone) was found using the Oxyblot protein oxidation detection kit.
source: Next, we utilized the Oxyblot protein oxidation detection kit to detect the carbonyl groups introduced into proteins by oxidative stress, and again found no evidence for increases in levels of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (DNP-hydrazone).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 with Oxyblot data.

claim: Fxn knockdown does not substantially or chronically elevate ROS in adult mice.
source: These finding provide evidence that Fxn knockdown does not substantially or chronically elevate ROS in adult mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the absence of ROS markers shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: 1959 genes were differentially expressed in Tg + mice heart when compared to Wt + and Tg - mice.
source: Differential expression analyses (Materials and methods) identified 1959 genes differentially expressed in Tg + mice heart when compared to Wt + and Tg - mice (FDR < 5%, Figure 7a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a with heatmap and stated in the text with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: 709 genes were differentially expressed in cerebellum of Tg + mice.
source: Similarly, we observed 709 and 206 genes differentially expressed in cerebellum and DRGs of Tg + mice, respectively (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b with summary data.

claim: 206 genes were differentially expressed in DRGs of Tg + mice.
source: Similarly, we observed 709 and 206 genes differentially expressed in cerebellum and DRGs of Tg + mice, respectively (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b with summary data.

claim: Only 31% of genes differentially expressed in the Tg + mice cerebellum were also dysregulated in heart.
source: Although cross tissue overlap in expression changes was significant, the majority of changes were tissue specific; only 31% and 38% of genes that were differentially expressed in the Tg + mice cerebellum and DRGs were also dysregulated in heart.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of the gene expression data.

claim: Only 38% of genes differentially expressed in the Tg + mice DRGs were also dysregulated in heart.
source: Although cross tissue overlap in expression changes was significant, the majority of changes were tissue specific; only 31% and 38% of genes that were differentially expressed in the Tg + mice cerebellum and DRGs were also dysregulated in heart.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of the gene expression data.

claim: Only 19% overlap was observed between differentially expressed genes in the DRG and cerebellum.
source: Likewise, we only observed a 19% overlap between differentially expressed genes in the DRG and cerebellum, consistent with previous observations that Fxn reduction causes distinct molecular changes in different tissues (Coppola et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Coppola et al., 2009.

claim: 38 genes involved in the chemokine signaling pathway were significantly differentially expressed due to Fxn knockdown in Tg + mice heart.
source: For example, 38 genes involved in the chemokine signaling pathway (KEGG: mmu04062) were significantly differentially expressed due to Fxn knockdown in Tg + mice heart (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 with heatmap data.

claim: Several genes involved in the chemokine signaling pathway (Ccl2, 3, 4, 7, Cxcl1, 16, Prkcd, Stat3) were consistently differentially expressed in six independent FRDA associated datasets.
source: Cross validating these genes with previously published gene expression datasets obtained from FRDA patients (Coppola et al., 2011) and mouse models associated with FRDA (Miranda et al., 2002; Puccio et al., 2001), identified several genes involved in the chemokine signaling pathway (E.g.: Ccl2, 3, 4, 7, Cxcl1, 16, Prkcd, Stat3) consistently differentially expressed in these six independent FRDA associated datasets (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations to Coppola et al., 2011, Miranda et al., 2002, and Puccio et al., 2001.

claim: 19 robust, reproducible co-expression modules were identified by WGCNA and consensus network analysis.
source: By applying WGCNA and consensus network analysis (Langfelder and Horvath, 2008; Chandran et al., 2016), we identified 19 robust, reproducible co-expression modules (Materials and methods; Figure 7—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 3) between the three tissues datasets generated at 0, 3, 12, 16 and 20 weeks after Fxn knockdown and 4 and 8 weeks post dox removal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 and supported by citations to Langfelder and Horvath, 2008 and Chandran et al., 2016.

claim: 11 modules were strongly associated with Fxn knockdown: three down-regulated modules in two or more tissues and three up-regulated modules.
source: Next, based on the significant module trait relationships (Wilcoxon p-value<0.05), we identified 11 modules strongly associated with Fxn knockdown: three down-regulated modules in two or more tissues after Fxn knockdown (yellow, lightgreen and turquoise) and three up-regulated modules (blue, purple, and black) (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 with module eigengene data.

claim: Three down-regulated modules in heart were up-regulated in cerebellum (red, greenyellow and magenta).
source: There also were three down-regulated modules in heart that were up-regulated in cerebellum (red, greenyellow and magenta) and two up-regulated modules in heart that were down-regulated in cerebellum (cyan and pink).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 with module eigengene data.

claim: Two up-regulated modules in heart were down-regulated in cerebellum (cyan and pink).
source: There also were three down-regulated modules in heart that were up-regulated in cerebellum (red, greenyellow and magenta) and two up-regulated modules in heart that were down-regulated in cerebellum (cyan and pink).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 with module eigengene data.

claim: Complement activation pathway genes (C3, C4b, C1qb, C1qc and Serping1) were up-regulated in the immune category.
source: For example, we show that immune, cell cycle and apoptosis related functional groups are up-regulated, whereas cardiac and mitochondrial related functional groups were down-regulated (Figure 7d). In the immune category, we observed most prominent changes in complement activation pathway genes, namely, C3, C4b, C1qb, C1qc and Serping1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d with network visualization.

claim: Many complement activation genes were also up-regulated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells obtained from FRDA patients.
source: Interesting, we also observed that many of these genes were also up-regulated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells obtained from FRDA patients (Figure 7—figure supplement 6), suggesting the potential for complement activation to act as a biomarker for FRDA as previously suggested for other degenerative diseases (Aiyaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6 and supported by citation to Aiyaz et al., 2012.

claim: Several genes related to cardiac function (Cacna2d1, Abcc9 and Hrc) were down-regulated in heart tissue upon frataxin knockdown.
source: Similarly, we found several genes, for example, Cacna2d1, Abcc9 and Hrc involved in normal cardiac function, to be down-regulated in heart tissue upon frataxin knockdown (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d with network visualization.

claim: CACNA2D1 is associated with Brugada syndrome.
source: CACNA2D1 is associated with Brugada syndrome, also known as sudden unexpected nocturnal death syndrome, a heart condition that causes ventricular arrhythmia (Risgaard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Risgaard et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in ABCC9 gene can cause dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: Mutations in ABCC9 gene can cause dilated cardiomyopathy (Bienengraeber et al., 2004) and a genetic variant in the HRC gene has been linked to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in dilated cardiomyopathy (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bienengraeber et al., 2004.

claim: A genetic variant in the HRC gene has been linked to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: Mutations in ABCC9 gene can cause dilated cardiomyopathy (Bienengraeber et al., 2004) and a genetic variant in the HRC gene has been linked to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in dilated cardiomyopathy (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2013.

claim: Genes related to apoptosis were up-regulated after Fxn knockdown in FRDAkd mice heart.
source: In agreement with this, we observed genes related to apoptosis were up-regulated after Fxn knockdown in FRDAkd mice heart (Figure 7d), which has been previously associated with FRDA pathogenesis and reported in other Fxn deficiency models (Simon et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2009; Bolinches-Amorós et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d and supported by citations to Simon et al., 2004, Huang et al., 2009, and Bolinches-Amorós et al., 2014.

claim: An increase in cleaved Caspase 8 protein levels was observed in Tg + heart tissue compared with control mice.
source: In order to validate our network findings, we tested CASP8 protein levels (Muzio et al., 1996), observing an increase in cleaved Caspase eight protein levels in Tg + heart tissue compared with control mice (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a with Western blot data and supported by citation to Muzio et al., 1996.

claim: No increase in cell death was observed in all tissues by TUNEL staining.
source: Next, we employed the TUNEL assay to detect apoptotic cells that undergo extensive DNA degradation during the late stages of apoptosis (Kyrylkova et al., 2012). However, we did not observe an increase in cell death in all tissues by TUNEL staining (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8b with TUNEL assay data and supported by citation to Kyrylkova et al., 2012.

claim: Several autophagy-related genes (Lamp2, Atf4, Tlr2, Optn, Mapk14, Sirt2, Icam1, Lgals3, Dcn, Rcan1, Grn) were present in disease phenotype-associated sub networks.
source: One pathway that was dysregulated and increasingly associated with neurodegeneration, was autophagy, since several autophagy-related genes (Lamp2, Atf4, Tlr2, Optn, Mapk14, Sirt2, Icam1, Lgals3, Dcn, Rcan1, Grn) were present in these disease phenotype-associated sub networks (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8c with network visualization.

claim: Autophagy activation was shown in Tg + mice heart using LC3-II as a marker.
source: To validate our network findings, we utilized LC3-II as a marker for autophagy, showing autophagy activation in Tg + mice heart, but not in spinal cord (Figure 8a,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a,d with Western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Autophagy was not activated in spinal cord of Tg + mice.
source: To validate our network findings, we utilized LC3-II as a marker for autophagy, showing autophagy activation in Tg + mice heart, but not in spinal cord (Figure 8a,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a,d with Western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Most of the gene expression changes observed in the symptomatic FRDAkd model are not recapitulated in two asymptomatic mouse models (KIKO and KIKI) with frataxin reduction below the threshold necessary to produce phenotype.
source: In contrast, in two asymptomatic mouse models (KIKO and KIKI) with frataxin reduction below the threshold necessary to produce phenotype (Miranda et al., 2002), most of the gene expression changes observed here in this symptomatic model are not recapitulated (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e with heatmap comparison and supported by citation to Miranda et al., 2002.

claim: Restoration of FXN expression in Fxn knockdown mice (Tg ±) led to significant improvement in lifespan with no death until 20 weeks post dox removal.
source: Restoration of FXN expression in Fxn knockdown mice (Tg ±) that had reached a level of substantial clinical dysfunction led to significant improvement in lifespan (no death until 20 weeks post dox removal) when compared to Tg + group, which resulted in a 90% mortality rate by 25 weeks after dox treatment initiation (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with survival curve data.

claim: Tg + group resulted in a 90% mortality rate by 25 weeks after dox treatment initiation.
source: Restoration of FXN expression in Fxn knockdown mice (Tg ±) that had reached a level of substantial clinical dysfunction led to significant improvement in lifespan (no death until 20 weeks post dox removal) when compared to Tg + group, which resulted in a 90% mortality rate by 25 weeks after dox treatment initiation (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with survival curve data.

claim: Rescue animals (Tg ±) displayed rapid improvement in gait ataxia, body weight, muscle strength, locomotor activity, and balance on rotarod test over 12 weeks.
source: Rescue animals (Tg ±) also displayed rapid improvement in: gait ataxia, body weight, muscle strength, locomotor activity, and balance on rotarod test over the ensuing 12 week period, to a point where the treated animals were not significantly different from controls on many tests (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with behavioral test data.

claim: All six FRDA associated clinical phenotypes tested showed significant improvement in rescue animals.
source: Remarkably, we observed all of the six FRDA associated clinical phenotypes tested showed significant improvement, suggesting that FRDA-like neurological defects due to absence of the mouse Fxn gene can be rectified by delayed restoration of Fxn (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with behavioral test data.

claim: Tg ± mice displayed reversal of the long QT interval phenotype after 12 weeks dox removal.
source: Tg ± mice that received the dox for 12 weeks followed by 12 weeks dox removal displayed reversal of the long QT interval phenotype, when compared to Tg + mice at both 12 and 24 weeks post dox treatment initiation (Figure 3a,b,e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a,b,e with ECG data.

claim: Ventricular and posterior wall thickening was observed only at 24 weeks post dox treatment in Tg + animals.
source: We observed ventricular and posterior wall thickening only at 24 weeks post dox treatment in Tg + animals (Figure 3d,f,g), suggesting that long QT interval phenotype is a earlier manifestation of disease that occurs before left ventricular wall thickening.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d,f,g with echocardiogram data.

claim: Long QT interval phenotype is an earlier manifestation of disease that occurs before left ventricular wall thickening.
source: We observed ventricular and posterior wall thickening only at 24 weeks post dox treatment in Tg + animals (Figure 3d,f,g), suggesting that long QT interval phenotype is a earlier manifestation of disease that occurs before left ventricular wall thickening.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal sequence of phenotypes observed in the data.

claim: Pathological and biochemical analyses in Tg ± mice heart following 8 weeks of dox withdrawal revealed improved cardiac function and reduced iron and ferritin accumulation, myocardial fibrosis, well-ordered sarcomeres, normal aconitase activity and reduced mitochondrial abnormalities.
source: Pathological and biochemical analyses in Tg ± mice heart following 8 weeks of dox withdrawal revealed improved cardiac function and reduced iron and ferritin accumulation, myocardial fibrosis, well-ordered sarcomeres, normal aconitase activity and reduced mitochondrial abnormalities (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with multiple pathological and biochemical assays.

claim: In the nervous system of Tg ± mice 8 weeks after dox removal, reduced empty vesicles and fewer condensed, degenerating mitochondria in DRG neurons were observed.
source: In the nervous system of Tg ± mice 8 weeks after dox removal, we observed reduced empty vesicles and fewer condensed, degenerating mitochondria in DRG neurons along with several abnormal mitochondria (empty and without cristae) containing DRG neurons compared with those in which dox was continued (Figure 5a–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a-f with electron microscopy data.

claim: Only mild improvement in myelin sheath thickness and cross section axonal size in the spinal cord of Tg ± mice was observed during the 8 week rescue period.
source: We only observed mild improvement in myelin sheath thickness and cross section axonal size in the spinal cord of Tg ± mice during this time period (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a-c with electron microscopy data.

claim: A significant reduction in the number of vacuoles and disrupted photoreceptors in the retina of Tg ± mice was observed.
source: Conversely, we observed a significant reduction in the number of vacuoles and disrupted photoreceptors in the retina of Tg ± mice, indicating that Fxn restoration rescued photoreceptor degeneration (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6d,e with electron microscopy data.

claim: After 8 weeks of dox removal following an initial 12 weeks of dox treatment, 100% normalization of gene expression levels was observed in cerebellum and DRGs.
source: After 8 weeks of dox removal following an initial 12 weeks of dox treatment, we examined the number of differentially expressed genes (at FDR < 5%) in all tissues and observed 100% normalization of gene expression levels in cerebellum and DRGs, and 99.95% of gene expression levels in the heart of FRDAkd mice (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a,b with gene expression data.

claim: 99.95% normalization of gene expression levels was observed in the heart of FRDAkd mice after rescue.
source: After 8 weeks of dox removal following an initial 12 weeks of dox treatment, we examined the number of differentially expressed genes (at FDR < 5%) in all tissues and observed 100% normalization of gene expression levels in cerebellum and DRGs, and 99.95% of gene expression levels in the heart of FRDAkd mice (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a,b with gene expression data.

claim: All six major behavioral deficits in FRDAkd mice were reversed.
source: In summary, all six major behavioral deficits in FRDAkd mice were reversed (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with behavioral test data.

claim: The long QT interval phenotype along with various pathological manifestations in the cardiac system were reversed.
source: In the cardiac system, the long QT interval phenotype along with various pathological manifestations, including mitochondrial defects were reversed.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3 and 4 with ECG and pathological data.

claim: Improvement in DRGs and photoreceptor neurons was observed in the nervous system after rescue.
source: In the nervous system, we observed improvement in DRGs and photoreceptor neurons, and complete reversal of the molecular changes in all three tissues suggesting near basal Fxn levels are sufficient to alleviate behavioral symptoms in the preclinical FRDAkd model.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5 and 6 with electron microscopy data.

claim: Complete reversal of molecular changes was observed in all three tissues after rescue.
source: In the nervous system, we observed improvement in DRGs and photoreceptor neurons, and complete reversal of the molecular changes in all three tissues suggesting near basal Fxn levels are sufficient to alleviate behavioral symptoms in the preclinical FRDAkd model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with gene expression data.

claim: Near basal Fxn levels are sufficient to alleviate behavioral symptoms in the preclinical FRDAkd model.
source: In the nervous system, we observed improvement in DRGs and photoreceptor neurons, and complete reversal of the molecular changes in all three tissues suggesting near basal Fxn levels are sufficient to alleviate behavioral symptoms in the preclinical FRDAkd model.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing restoration of Fxn levels leads to phenotype reversal.

claim: Restoration of Fxn expression, even after the development of severe symptoms and pathological defects, resulted in drastic amelioration of the clinical phenotype in both cardiac and nervous systems.
source: Importantly, restoration of Fxn expression, even after the development of severe symptoms and pathological defects, resulted in a drastic amelioration of the clinical phenotype, both in the cardiac and nervous systems, including motor activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pathology was significantly improved in the heart, DRGs and in the retina after Fxn restoration.
source: Pathology was significantly improved in the heart, DRGs and in the retina, but only mild improvement was observed in spinal cord, suggesting Fxn restoration for the duration of 8 weeks is not sufficient for reversal of neuronal defects in the spinal cord after Fxn knockdown.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4-6 with pathological data.

claim: Fxn restoration for 8 weeks is not sufficient for reversal of neuronal defects in the spinal cord after Fxn knockdown.
source: Pathology was significantly improved in the heart, DRGs and in the retina, but only mild improvement was observed in spinal cord, suggesting Fxn restoration for the duration of 8 weeks is not sufficient for reversal of neuronal defects in the spinal cord after Fxn knockdown.
evidence: This is inferred from the limited improvement observed in spinal cord compared to other tissues.

claim: Transcriptomic changes due to Fxn knockdown in three different tissues differed.
source: Interestingly, transcriptomic changes due to Fxn knockdown in three different tissues differed (Coppola et al., 2009), indicating variable response to frataxin deficiency, which could partly explain cell and tissue selectivity in FRDA (Lynch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations to Coppola et al., 2009 and Lynch et al., 2012.

claim: Variable response to frataxin deficiency could partly explain cell and tissue selectivity in FRDA.
source: Interestingly, transcriptomic changes due to Fxn knockdown in three different tissues differed (Coppola et al., 2009), indicating variable response to frataxin deficiency, which could partly explain cell and tissue selectivity in FRDA (Lynch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific gene expression changes and supported by citation to Lynch et al., 2012.

claim: The onset and progression of the disease correlates with the concentration of doxycycline (shRNA induction).
source: The onset and progression of the disease correlates with the concentration of doxycycline (shRNA induction), and the phenotype returns to baseline after its withdrawal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments and rescue experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The phenotype returns to baseline after doxycycline withdrawal.
source: The onset and progression of the disease correlates with the concentration of doxycycline (shRNA induction), and the phenotype returns to baseline after its withdrawal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The FRDAkd model exhibits several unique features that provide advantages for the study of FRDA pathophysiology relative to other existing models.
source: This new FRDAkd model exhibits several unique features that provide advantages for the study of FRDA pathophysiology relative to other existing models (Miranda et al., 2002; Al-Mahdawi et al., 2004; Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006; Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004; Perdomini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison to other models cited.

claim: Induction of frataxin knockdown permits circumventing potential confounding developmental effects.
source: First, induction of frataxin knockdown permits circumventing potential confounding developmental effects (Cossée et al., 2000) and has the flexibility to enhance the disease onset and progression very rapidly by increasing the doxycycline dose.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Cossée et al., 2000.

claim: The model has flexibility to enhance disease onset and progression rapidly by increasing doxycycline dose.
source: First, induction of frataxin knockdown permits circumventing potential confounding developmental effects (Cossée et al., 2000) and has the flexibility to enhance the disease onset and progression very rapidly by increasing the doxycycline dose.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments described in the methods.

claim: Reversibility of Fxn knockdown provides a unique model to mimic the effect of an ideal therapeutic intervention.
source: Second, reversibility of Fxn knockdown provides a unique model to mimic the effect of an ideal therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and demonstrated by rescue experiments.

claim: The doxycycline-dependent reduction of Fxn expression can be tailored to determine the critical threshold of Fxn levels necessary to induce selective cellular dysfunction.
source: Third, the doxycycline-dependent reduction of Fxn expression can be tailored to carefully determine the critical threshold of Fxn levels necessary to induce selective cellular dysfunction in the nervous system (DRGs and spinal cord) and to understand the occurrence of tissue specific dysfunction in FRDA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a potential application of the model.

claim: The temporal control of single copy and reversible regulation of shRNA expression produces reproducible transgene expression from the rosa26 locus.
source: Finally, the temporal control of single copy and reversible regulation of shRNA expression against Fxn produces reproducible transgene expression from the well-characterized rosa26 locus to generate the first model to exhibit and reverse several symptoms parallel to FRDA patients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and demonstrated by the experimental data.

claim: This is the first model to exhibit and reverse several symptoms parallel to FRDA patients.
source: Finally, the temporal control of single copy and reversible regulation of shRNA expression against Fxn produces reproducible transgene expression from the well-characterized rosa26 locus to generate the first model to exhibit and reverse several symptoms parallel to FRDA patients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on comparison to other models.

claim: FRDAkd animals are defective in several behaviors including weight loss, reduced locomotor activity, reduced strength, ataxia and early mortality.
source: We show that FRDAkd animals are defective in several behaviors and exhibit weight loss, reduced locomotor activity, reduced strength, ataxia and early mortality.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with behavioral test data.

claim: All behavioral defects were significantly improved following Fxn restoration, approaching or reaching wild-type levels.
source: All of these defects were significantly improved following Fxn restoration, approaching or reaching wild-type levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with rescue experiment data.

claim: Ataxia and survival are well-established and important clinical endpoints in FRDA.
source: Most importantly ataxia and survival are well-established and important clinical endpoints in FRDA (Tsou et al., 2011), readouts after Fxn restoration clearly improve these parameters and appear to be directly related to the functional status of the FRDAkd mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsou et al., 2011.

claim: Fxn deficient mice exhibit considerable neurological plasticity even in a nervous system that is fully adult.
source: We conclude that Fxn deficient mice exhibit considerable neurological plasticity even in a nervous system that is fully adult.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing recovery of neurological function in adult mice.

claim: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common clinical feature in FRDA.
source: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common clinical feature in FRDA and approximately 60% of patients with typical childhood onset FRDA die from cardiac failure (Tsou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsou et al., 2011.

claim: Approximately 60% of patients with typical childhood onset FRDA die from cardiac failure.
source: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common clinical feature in FRDA and approximately 60% of patients with typical childhood onset FRDA die from cardiac failure (Tsou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsou et al., 2011.

claim: Cardiac failure is believed to be caused by the loss of cardiomyocytes through activation of apoptosis.
source: It is generally believed that cardiac failure is caused by the loss of cardiomyocytes through activation of apoptosis (Fujita and Ishikawa, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fujita and Ishikawa, 2011.

claim: Activation of early apoptosis pathways was observed in heart tissue of FRDAkd mice.
source: We observed activation of early apoptosis pathways in heart tissue and severe cardiomyopathy characterized by ventricular wall thickness (Bennett, 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7 and 8 with gene expression and Western blot data, and supported by citation to Bennett, 2002.

claim: Enhanced activation of autophagy was observed in the heart tissue of FRDAkd mice.
source: We also observed enhanced activation of autophagy in the heart tissue of FRDAkd mice, where autophagic cardiomyocytes are observed at a significantly higher frequency during cardiac failure (Martinet et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with LC3 staining data and supported by citation to Martinet et al., 2007.

claim: Apoptosis and autophagy together might synergistically play a vital role in the development of cardiac defect in FRDA.
source: These results suggest that apoptosis and autophagy together might synergistically play a vital role in the development of cardiac defect in FRDA (Eisenberg-Lerner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both pathways being activated and supported by citation to Eisenberg-Lerner et al., 2009.

claim: FRDAkd mice initially exhibited a long QT interval at 12 weeks, followed by absence of P-waves and increased ventricular wall thickness at 24 weeks.
source: During Fxn knockdown, FRDAkd mice initially exhibited a long QT interval at 12 weeks during electrocardiographic analyses, followed by the absence of P-waves and increased ventricular wall thickness at 24 weeks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 with ECG and echocardiogram data.

claim: Restoration of Fxn levels at 12 weeks reversed long QT interval phenotype.
source: Restoration of Fxn levels at 12 weeks reversed long QT interval phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 with ECG data from rescue animals.

claim: Iron accumulation and deficiency in aconitase activity are prominent features of Fxn deficiency in cardiac muscle.
source: Another prominent feature of Fxn deficiency mouse and FRDA patients is iron accumulation and deficiency in activity of the iron-sulfur cluster dependent enzyme, aconitase, in cardiac muscle (Puccio et al., 2001; Rötig et al., 1997; Delatycki et al., 1999; Michael et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puccio et al., 2001, Rötig et al., 1997, Delatycki et al., 1999, and Michael et al., 2006.

claim: Increased iron accumulation and reduced aconitase activity were observed in the cardiac tissue of FRDAkd mice.
source: Consistent with these observations, we observed increased iron accumulation and reduced aconitase activity in the cardiac tissue of FRDAkd mice and we demonstrate a marked reversal of both to a statistically significant extent, suggesting Fxn restoration is sufficient to overcome and clear the iron accumulation and reverse aconitase activity (Tan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with iron staining and aconitase activity data, and supported by citation to Tan et al., 2001.

claim: Fxn restoration is sufficient to overcome and clear iron accumulation and reverse aconitase activity.
source: Consistent with these observations, we observed increased iron accumulation and reduced aconitase activity in the cardiac tissue of FRDAkd mice and we demonstrate a marked reversal of both to a statistically significant extent, suggesting Fxn restoration is sufficient to overcome and clear the iron accumulation and reverse aconitase activity (Tan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with rescue experiment data and supported by citation to Tan et al., 2001.

claim: Several genes directly involved in hemochromatosis and iron overload (Hfe, Slc40a1, Hmox1, Tfrc and Gdf15) were upregulated in FRDAkd mice.
source: Our gene expression data revealed several genes (Hfe [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012], Slc40a1 [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012], Hmox1 [Song et al., 2012], Tfrc [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012] and Gdf15 [Cui et al., 2014]) directly involved in hemochromatosis and iron overload to be upregulated in our FRDAkd mice, all of which were rescued to normal levels by frataxin restoration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with gene expression data and supported by multiple citations.

claim: All iron metabolism genes upregulated in FRDAkd mice were rescued to normal levels by frataxin restoration.
source: Our gene expression data revealed several genes (Hfe [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012], Slc40a1 [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012], Hmox1 [Song et al., 2012], Tfrc [Del-Castillo-Rueda et al., 2012] and Gdf15 [Cui et al., 2014]) directly involved in hemochromatosis and iron overload to be upregulated in our FRDAkd mice, all of which were rescued to normal levels by frataxin restoration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with gene expression data from rescue animals.

claim: Several downregulated genes involved in normal cardiac function (Cacna2D1, Abcc9 and Hrc) were rescued by Fxn restoration.
source: Similarly, several downregulated genes involved in normal cardiac function (Cacna2D1, Abcc9 and Hrc) were rescued by Fxn restoration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with gene expression data from rescue animals.

claim: Fxn restoration in symptomatic FRDAkd mice reverses the early development of cardiomyopathy at the molecular, cellular and physiological levels.
source: Together, these data indicate that Fxn restoration in symptomatic FRDAkd mice reverses the early development of cardiomyopathy at the molecular, cellular and physiological levels.
evidence: This is based on the comprehensive rescue data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 7.

claim: Cellular dysfunction due to FXN deficiency is presumed to be the result of a mitochondrial defect.
source: Cellular dysfunction due to FXN deficiency is presumed to be the result of a mitochondrial defect, since FXN localizes to mitochondria (Tan et al., 2001; Koutnikova et al., 1997; Foury and Cazzalini, 1997) and deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes and function have been observed in tissues of FRDA patients (Rötig et al., 1997; Lodi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on FXN localization and mitochondrial function.

claim: FXN localizes to mitochondria.
source: Cellular dysfunction due to FXN deficiency is presumed to be the result of a mitochondrial defect, since FXN localizes to mitochondria (Tan et al., 2001; Koutnikova et al., 1997; Foury and Cazzalini, 1997) and deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes and function have been observed in tissues of FRDA patients (Rötig et al., 1997; Lodi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2001, Koutnikova et al., 1997, and Foury and Cazzalini, 1997.

claim: Deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes and function have been observed in tissues of FRDA patients.
source: Cellular dysfunction due to FXN deficiency is presumed to be the result of a mitochondrial defect, since FXN localizes to mitochondria (Tan et al., 2001; Koutnikova et al., 1997; Foury and Cazzalini, 1997) and deficiencies of mitochondrial enzymes and function have been observed in tissues of FRDA patients (Rötig et al., 1997; Lodi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rötig et al., 1997 and Lodi et al., 1999.

claim: It has been hypothesized that FXN deficiency induced mitochondrial dysfunction involves the production of ROS.
source: It has been hypothesized that FXN deficiency induced mitochondrial dysfunction involves the production of ROS, which subsequently lead to cellular dysfunction (Tamarit et al., 2016; Santos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tamarit et al., 2016 and Santos et al., 2010.

claim: Several studies have suggested the existence of ROS markers in FRDA patient samples.
source: Several studies have suggested the existence of ROS markers in FRDA patient samples (Schulz et al., 2000; Tozzi et al., 2002; Piemonte et al., 2001; Emond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Other evidence from several different FRDA model organisms suggests that ROS are not elevated.
source: However, other evidence from several different FRDA model organisms suggests that ROS are not elevated (Chen et al., 2016a; Chen et al., 2016b; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010) and more than ten clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients (Kearney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and clinical trials.

claim: More than ten clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients.
source: However, other evidence from several different FRDA model organisms suggests that ROS are not elevated (Chen et al., 2016a; Chen et al., 2016b; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010) and more than ten clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy have shown no or limited benefit in FRDA patients (Kearney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kearney et al., 2012.

claim: FRDAkd mice displayed accumulation of damaged mitochondria and reduced aconitase as a direct consequence of frataxin deficiency in heart.
source: Here we show that FRDAkd mice displayed accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and reduced aconitase as a direct consequence of frataxin deficiency in heart, consistent with previous findings in conditional FRDA mouse models (Puccio et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2004).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with electron microscopy and biochemical data, and supported by citations to Puccio et al., 2001 and Simon et al., 2004.

claim: Frataxin deficiency inhibits mitochondrial function leading to cellular dysfunction.
source: This is consistent with the model whereby frataxin deficiency inhibits mitochondrial function leading to cellular dysfunction (González-Cabo and Palau, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to González-Cabo and Palau, 2013.

claim: Restoration of FXN resulted in improvement in pathological mitochondrial structure.
source: Restoration of FXN resulted in improvement in pathological mitochondrial structure indicating that FXN restoration prevents mitochondrial defects and may thereby enhance cell survival (Tan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with electron microscopy data from rescue animals and supported by citation to Tan et al., 2001.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction recovery occurred as early as eight weeks after FXN restoration.
source: Our observation of mitochondrial dysfunction recovery as early as eight weeks after FXN restoration is consistent with the highly dynamic nature of mitochondrial function (Chan, 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with rescue experiment data and supported by citation to Chan, 2012.

claim: Higher level of condensed mitochondria was observed in DRGs through ultrastructural analyses.
source: In the nervous system, we observed higher level of condensed mitochondria in DRGs through ultrastructural analyses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with electron microscopy data.

claim: Condensed mitochondria are known to have lower respiratory control and ATP production.
source: Condensed mitochondria are known to have lower respiratory control and ATP production (Desagher and Martinou, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desagher and Martinou, 2000.

claim: Condensed mitochondria in DRG neurons of FRDAkd mice were associated with electron-light, or 'empty' vesicles.
source: On most occasions, these condensed mitochondria in DRG neurons of FRDAkd mice were associated with electron-light, or 'empty' vesicles.
